blocks.explanation:
Parametric equations; show that \(y_{2} = -2\).
Plan: \(y_{1} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\), then \(y_{2} = \frac{d}{dt}(y_{1})\cdot\frac{dt}{dx}\).
steps:
Given: \(x = \sin t\), \(y = \cos^{2}t\).
To prove: \(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + 2 = 0\).
Method: parametric differentiation twice.

Derivatives with respect to \(t\)
\[\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \cos t\]
\[\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 2\cos t(-\sin t) = -2\sin t\cos t\]
Why: chain rule on \(\cos^{2}t = (\cos t)^{2}\).

First derivative
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{-2\sin t\cos t}{\cos t} = -2\sin t\]
Why: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\), with \(\cos t \ne 0\).

Second derivative
\[\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(-2\sin t)\cdot\dfrac{dt}{dx}\]
\[= -2\cos t\cdot\dfrac{1}{\cos t} = -2\]
\[\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} + 2 = 0\]
Why: \(\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{1}{\cos t}\).
